scenarios.title: Checkout stops mid-handshake
scenarios.story: It is 9:40 on a Monday. Your team runs the checkout service for a mid-size online store. At 9:37 every payment started failing — not some, all of them. The on-call channel pings you: orders have dropped to zero and the first customer tickets are arriving. You are the on-call engineer.

services.name: Checkout API
services.role: takes the cart and charges the card

services.name: Payment gateway
services.role: bank-side service that runs the charge

services.name: Edge CDN
services.role: serves the storefront itself

services.name: Metrics stack
services.role: dashboards and alerts

timeline.text: Alert: checkout success rate fell from 99.2% to 0% in two minutes. Severity: SEV-1.

reveal.title: Checkout API — golden signals
lines: requests/sec: 420 → 38 (dropping)
latency p95: 210ms — normal for this hour
error rate: responses ending in TLS alerts, not HTTP errors
payment-gateway: green, latency normal
cli browsed the storefront fine — only the charge step fails

reveal.title: checkout-api/error.log — last 10 minutes
lines: 09:38:02 – handshake failed: certificate verify failed (certificate expired)
09:38:04 – handshake failed: certificate verify failed (certificate expired)
09:39:11 – upstream charge aborted: TLS layer rejected before HTTP
09:39:40 – certificate verify failed (certificate expired) — 4,214 occurrences this hour

reveal.title: Changes — last 7 days
lines: deploys to checkout-api: none in 6 days (last: 2026-11-03, config-only)
payment-gateway: no version change for 3 weeks
infrastructure: certificate auto-renewal job ran 'last week' per schedule — logged exit code 1

reveal.title: Cross-service comparison, 09:30–09:45
lines: payment-gateway: healthy from its own logs, accepting test charges fine
cdn-edge: certificate presented is different and valid (expires in 61 days)
checkout-api certificate: issuer 'StoreFront CA', notAfter = yesterday 23:59
failure starts exactly when that certificate crossed its expiry

reveal.title: Manual check against checkout-api
lines: > verify certificate on checkout-api:443
subject: storename.example
issuer: StoreFront CA
notAfter: yesterday 23:59 UTC — EXPIRED
auto-renewal path on disk: missing (job failed last week, no retry configured)

reveal.title: Rollback attempt
lines: nothing to roll back — checkout-api has had no deploy for 6 days
lock on deploy pipeline acquired and released; 10 minutes of the incident spent

reveal.title: Scaling result
lines: 3 new instances came up healthy
all 5 instances now fail the same TLS handshake — same expired certificate on each
payment-gateway now sees 5x the retry traffic from us

rootCauses.label: The TLS certificate on checkout-api expired last night, so every charge is refused before HTTP
The payment gateway is down or refusing charges
A typo in last week's config rollout broke checkout
A traffic spike is overwhelming checkout

fixes.label: Reissue the certificate, deploy it to all checkout instances, and fix the renewal job with an expiry alert
fixes.note: Root cause addressed, plus a guard so the same night does not repeat — this is the fix the real team's postmortem pointed to.

fixes.label: Roll back the most recent deploy
fixes.note: There was no deploy — the certificate stays expired and checkout stays down.

fixes.label: Scale checkout out 5x to push through the errors
fixes.note: Every new instance carries the same expired certificate. You add load to the payment gateway and fix nothing.

hintLadder: The dashboard shows requests failing while latency stays normal — that combination points away from load. Look at where exactly the requests die.
The logs name a very specific TLS problem. One cheap, safe check confirms the state of a certificate directly.
The failing certificate and the healthy CDN certificate are different files. Check when the checkout one expired, and who was supposed to renew it.

guidance.text: Start with the dashboard: does this look like load, latency, or errors? The answer narrows everything after.
Errors at the TLS layer usually mean one of two things: a certificate problem or a recent change. The logs and the change list will tell you which.
When you suspect a certificate, verify it directly — checking expiry is safe, cheap, and impossible to argue with.

defendQuestions.question: Why did every payment fail at once instead of a few users seeing errors?
Scaling out made nothing better. Why, in terms of the certificate?
What would you change so this class of failure announces itself before users do?

scenarios.lesson: Certificates expire on a calendar, not on usage — and they fail closed. A quiet renewal job with a non-zero exit and no retry is a live incident waiting for its date. Alert on expiry windows, not on broken handshakes.
scenarios.realAction: In the real incident, the service's authentication certificate expired and locked users out for hours; the company said afterwards that an authentication certificate had expired and they were rotating it, adding expiry monitoring so the failure could not repeat silently. We simplified the scale: one service, one store, synthetic numbers.

source.title: Microsoft Teams has been down this morning (TechCrunch, quoting Microsoft)

scenarios.title: A maintenance typo takes out object storage
scenarios.story: You are on-call for a large object-storage platform. At 9:37 am the scheduled maintenance playbook ran, and minutes later a third of the platform's requests started failing — and this platform backs half the web, so within minutes customer tickets and public reports pile up. The last maintenance step removed some expired servers from the index. Something in that step went wrong.

services.name: Storage index
services.role: tracks every storage node and allocates capacity

services.name: Storage nodes
services.role: hold the data itself

services.name: Platform dashboards
services.role: status pages and metrics — served from this same storage

services.name: Customer apps
services.role: customer services reading and writing files

timeline.text: Alert: error rate for object operations in the primary region jumped from 0.01% to 33%.

events.text: Customer apps start timing out and retrying; their back-off is not working for some, so retry traffic multiplies.
Your own dashboards and status page stop loading — they read from this storage system.

reveal.title: Primary region — object operations
lines: GET/PUT error rate: 0.01% → 33% and climbing
affected operations: reads and writes both, one region only
other regions: green, no error change
internal dashboards: partially degraded (they host their own files here)

reveal.title: storage-index/maintenance.log — this morning
lines: 09:37:12 – playbook 'expire-old-servers' started (scheduled)
09:37:41 – subsystem REMOVE ran: 'removing a set of expired server entries from the index'
09:37:44 – index health: storage-node pool below minimum healthy threshold
09:37:52 – warnings: allocation requests have no free server to place data on

actions.label: Inspect the exact change list from maintenance

reveal.title: Maintenance change detail
lines: intended playbook input: remove 1 expired test server entry
actual input: one additional character in the server list argument
result: 27 entries removed instead of 1 — the index now records a far smaller pool than reality
change was applied to the live index without a dry-run step

actions.label: Compare capacity metrics before and after

reveal.title: Index pool utilization
lines: 09:30 — recorded pool: 410 nodes, utilization 34%
09:38 — recorded pool: 383 nodes, utilization 96%
actual physical nodes online: 409 (they never went anywhere)
the data still exists on disk; only the index's view of the pool collapsed

actions.label: Check DNS resolution for the storage endpoints

reveal.title: DNS spot checks
lines: all storage endpoints resolve correctly from 4 vantage points
TTLs and records unchanged in 30 days — tempting to check, genuinely fine
errors are application-level 'capacity' errors, not DNS failure

reveal.title: Index restart
lines: index restarted cleanly from ITS OWN recorded state
recorded state is the problem: pool still shows 383 nodes, utilization 96%
error rate unchanged; 10 sim-minutes spent

actions.label: Escalate: declare SEV-1 and pull in the platform coordinator

reveal.title: On-call coordination
lines: coordinator joins; comms channel opened; cross-team work streamed (this regional dependency is bigger than one queue)
real time-out: severity page and public comms also depend on helpers because your own dashboards are degraded

rootCauses.label: A one-character typo in the removal input stripped far more server entries from the index than intended, so allocation believed most of the pool was gone
A DNS problem is sending clients to dead endpoints
A customer's viral app spiked traffic past capacity
A wave of disk failures removed real storage capacity

fixes.label: Restore the removed index entries from the index configuration backup and re-run allocation
fixes.note: The data never left disk; rebuilding the index's view restores placement. This mirrors what the real team did: restart with a correct, smaller set of steps and let the subsystem rebuild capacity from its records.

fixes.label: Let the autoscaler add new nodes until the pool recovers
fixes.note: Provisioning a third of a region takes days. The index is lying about existing nodes — new ones do not fix the view.

fixes.label: Delete the index and rebuild it from scratch to fix the corruption
fixes.note: You do not rebuild the one component every request consults during an outage. It prolongs the incident and risks the entry data you need for recovery.

hintLadder: One region only, both reads and writes — that points at something all operations share, not at any single customer or disk.
The maintenance window and the failure start line up to the minute. What exactly did the playbook change, and what does its change record show?
Compare what the index believes (its recorded pool) against what physically exists. If they disagree, the fix is about the index's view, not the hardware.

defendQuestions.question: Retries from customer apps made the outage worse. Why did their retries multiply the damage?
Why did waiting on the autoscaler fail as a strategy here?
The dashboards themselves went down. What does that tell you to change for next time?

scenarios.lesson: The bigger the blast radius of a maintenance tool, the more its inputs deserve a dry-run, a size guard, and a human-readable preview. 'Remove 1' and 'remove 27' should not both pass without a pause.
scenarios.realAction: In the real incident, a mistyped command made a maintenance subsystem remove a much larger set of server entries than intended; capacity plummeted, retries cascaded across customer applications, and even the company's own dashboards degraded because they depended on the affected storage. Recovery meant restoring the index and letting capacity rebuild. We simplified to one typo, one region, synthetic numbers.

source.title: Summary of the Amazon S3 Service Disruption in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region

scenarios.inspiredByNote: Inspired by AWS's public postmortem of the February 2017 S3 disruption, simplified. Every log line and number is synthetic.

scenarios.title: The tagging model starts labeling people wrongly
scenarios.story: You are the on-call for a photo app's ML platform. At 8 am the human-review queue reports that new uploads are getting an offensive, wildly wrong label for a group of users, and the overnight evaluation alert fired: accuracy for one label family collapsed after the nightly retrain. Users are already posting screenshots. You need to find what changed and stop the harm.

services.name: Labeling model
services.role: assigns tags to uploaded photos

services.name: Training pipeline
services.role: nightly retrain on new labeled data

services.name: Evaluation service
services.role: runs held-out quality checks after each retrain

services.name: Human review queue
services.role: flagged predictions reviewed by people

timeline.text: Alert: overnight evaluation failed — label-class accuracy for one family dropped from 99.1% to 71.4%. Two user reports of offensive tags arrived in the same window.

events.text: A user posts a screenshot of a wrong label on a public forum; staff confirm the report is real.
The review queue floods: hundreds of photos flagged by users for the same label family.

reveal.title: Overnight eval — per-class accuracy
lines: class 'animal-family': accuracy 99.1% (unchanged)
class 'c-people': accuracy 71.4% — was 99.0% yesterday
overall model accuracy: 98.7% — barely moved (one class collapsed)
eval ran on the same held-out set as always — the benchmark itself is fine

reveal.title: labeling-model/serve.log — this morning
lines: model version in production: same as yesterday (deploy was 5 days ago)
request latency and error rates: normal
wrong-label predictions show ordinary, confident model outputs — no crash, no fallback path
mislabels cluster on photos containing the same subject type

reveal.title: Platform changes — last 48 hours
lines: model deploys: none for 5 days
serving config: unchanged
training pipeline: nightly retrain job ran 02:00; a new data source bucket was added to the ingestion config 2 days ago
the new bucket passed only a pipeline-smoke check, not a label-quality review

reveal.title: Nightly training batch composition
lines: batch size: 2.4M labeled images (usual: 300K)
new source bucket contributed 2.1M of them — added without label review
random sample of 50 from the new bucket: 11 labels are wrong, 3 are abusive
the mislabeled rows correlate exactly with the eval class that collapsed

actions.label: Run a safe sample check on live predictions

reveal.title: Manual sample — 100 fresh uploads
lines: 9 of 100 uploads carry the wrong label; every one contains the same subject type
confidence scores are high — the model is sure, and wrong
serving stack is healthy; the model's judgment is the thing that changed

reveal.title: Feature flag: auto-tag OFF
lines: no new labels are generated; user-facing harm stops growing
uploads continue; labels queue for later human pass
this is containment, not the fix — the poisoned batch is still in the model

actions.label: Roll back to the previous model build

reveal.title: Model rollback
lines: previous build restored; the immediate mislabels stop
that build was trained on the same pipeline — tomorrow's retrain will re-learn from the same poisoned bucket
rollback treats the symptom, not the source

actions.label: Escalate: bring in the safety review queue and notify the platform lead

reveal.title: Escalation
lines: trust-and-safety reviewers start an emergency label pass on flagged uploads
platform lead wakes the data- ingestion owner; public-response draft started
an ML quality incident with user-facing harm needs humans in the loop, not just an engineer

rootCauses.label: A newly added, unreviewed data source poured mislabeled images into the nightly training batch, and the retrained model learned the wrong associations
A bug in the last model deploy broke predictions for that class
Real-world photo content drifted faster than the model could handle
The evaluation benchmark itself is broken and the alarm is a false one

fixes.label: Keep tagging paused, remove the unreviewed source, retrain on verified data, and add a label-quality gate before any new source can enter training
fixes.note: Contains the harm, removes the cause, and adds the missing check so an unreviewed bucket cannot reach training again.

fixes.label: Restore the previous model build and move on
fixes.note: The pipeline that poisoned last night's batch will poison tonight's too. Nothing upstream changed.

fixes.label: Ship an emergency filter that hides just the offensive label word everywhere
fixes.note: It silences the visible symptom and leaves the model blind to a whole concept — the kind of shortcut that reads as a fix today and becomes its own incident later.

hintLadder: One class collapsed while overall accuracy barely moved — that is a data story, not an infrastructure story.
The model in production did not change for five days. Ask instead what the model learned from overnight.
Compare the new training batch against the usual one — size, sources, and who (or what) reviewed the labels.

defendQuestions.question: Why did rolling back the model not fix the root cause?
You paused auto-tagging first instead of fixing the model. Why is containment worth it even before the cause is known?
What gate belongs between any new data source and the training set?

scenarios.lesson: A model is only as trustworthy as the pipeline that feeds it. Any data source must clear the same quality bar as the code that ships — reviewed, sampled, and gated — because bad labels do not crash anything; they quietly become behavior.
scenarios.realAction: In the real incident, a widely used photo app mislabeled a group of people with an offensive tag; the company apologized publicly, said it was appalled, and worked on labels for that class. Follow-up reporting years later found the visible label had been blocked rather than fully fixed, which is exactly the shortcut our edge teaches against. We changed the cause to an unreviewed data source and made every number synthetic.

source.title: When It Comes to Gorillas, Google Photos Remains Blind (WIRED)

scenarios.inspiredByNote: Inspired by Google Photos' publicly reported 2015 labeling failure and its public follow-up, simplified. Every model, dataset, and number is synthetic.

scenarios.title: Verified accounts start posting a scam
scenarios.story: You are the on-call for platform security at a social platform. At 3:02 pm, reports flood in: several well-known verified accounts are posting the same cryptocurrency scam, one after another. Nothing was deployed today. Your job is purely defensive: figure out how the accounts are being abused and contain it, then say what you would harden.

services.name: Auth service
services.role: logins, password resets, sessions

services.name: Internal support tools
services.role: let support staff act on accounts

services.name: Posting API
services.role: publishes posts from apps and internal tools

services.name: Support desk
services.role: first to see user reports

timeline.text: Alert from the support desk: 6+ high-profile accounts posted the same scam post within minutes. Screenshots included. Nothing deployed today.

events.text: Two more verified accounts post the same scam; press notices.
Your integrity team asks for a answer: is this the app, the accounts, or our own tooling?

reveal.title: Support desk — scam reports
lines: reports of the same scam post: 9 high-profile accounts, 14 minutes
all posts carry identical text; users flag them within a minute of posting
no new tickets about password problems from those accounts' owners
support can still log in and work — the abuse is specific, not general

reveal.title: auth-service/audit.log — this afternoon
lines: 14:22 – password reset approved by the phone-based reset desk for 2 internal accounts
14:31 – those accounts logged in from 2 new networks, SMS second factor accepted
14:33 – MFA push approval in under 4 seconds — user was on a live call at the time (per calendar)
no failed-attempt bursts anywhere: this was not a credentials guess, it was credentials handed over

actions.label: Check today's change and deploy log

reveal.title: Changes — platform, last 24 hours
lines: deployments: none today (last deploy: 4 days ago, no auth changes in it)
auth config: unchanged for 3 weeks
nothing about today's failure involves new code

actions.label: Trace what the internal tools did under those sessions

reveal.title: admin-tools/audit.log — 14:33 onward
lines: 14:34 – 'delegate posting access' granted from staff session S-114 → target verified accounts (9 in 11 minutes)
14:36 – posts published via a path that reflects staff-tool provenance, not the public apps
the tool trusted the staff session fully; a support-level login could reach these actions at all
all 9 scam posts trace back through delegate grants, not through any of the owners' own devices

actions.label: Inspect posting-API traffic for leaked credentials

reveal.title: Posting API — credential path analysis
lines: posts in question: all authorized by staff-tool delegate tokens, none by app client credentials
no single API key in use across the 9 posts; app credentials nowhere in the chain
posting API itself: functioned exactly per its rules — the rules were the problem

actions.label: Run a live session inventory for the affected staff accounts

reveal.title: Active sessions — 2 staff accounts
lines: each account shows 2 live sessions right now: office + unknown network
unknown networks match the 14:31 logins exactly
delegate grants from those sessions: 9, all revocable from this console

actions.label: Force a password rotation on the two staff accounts

reveal.title: Credential rotation
lines: passwords rotated; the desk plans to re-verify the humans later
existing sessions survive a rotation and stay logged in by design
one more scam post just went out — rotation alone did not contain anything

actions.label: Revoke the live sessions and every delegate grant they created

reveal.title: Session + grant revocation
lines: both unknown-network sessions terminated; 9 delegate grants revoked
posting through the internal path stops; owners' own apps unaffected (their sessions were never touched)
support's legitimate access continues through a fresh login — least privilege would say the tool should not have allowed this in the first place

actions.label: Escalate: declare a security incident and pull in integrity + comms

reveal.title: Incident declaration
lines: security incident declared; integrity team joins; owner-outreach list assembled
comms drafts the public note; platform lead restricted some account features platform-wide during response, as the real incident did
the reset desk pauses phone-based resets until the process is re-verified — the path that was abused

rootCauses.label: Staff were tricked by phone-based social engineering into resetting credentials, and the attackers used that access with internal tools to post and delegate over these accounts
A leaked API key lets outsiders post directly
A recent deploy quietly weakened authentication
An employee is deliberately posting the scams

fixes.label: Revoke every affected session and delegate grant, force credential resets with phishing-resistant MFA, restrict the internal tool's override path pending review, and add voice-verification for password resets
fixes.note: Contain first, then close the specific path that was abused, then make the same trick structurally harder. This mirrors the real response: sessions and access were cut and the platform limited the affected surfaces during the incident.

fixes.label: Delete the scam posts and suspend the affected accounts
fixes.note: The attackers still hold access and the accounts are victims — deleting posts removes evidence and restores nothing while new scam posts go out.

fixes.label: Take posting offline platform-wide until you fully understand the incident
fixes.note: A contained, targeted problem does not justify taking the entire platform's voice offline — the blast radius should match the blast.

hintLadder: Nothing new shipped and the pattern hits famous accounts first — check how access is gained, not what code runs.
Password resets sound harmless in logs. Check who could be talked into approving one, and what the reset process actually verifies.
Compare the few compromised accounts' session trail to everyone else's. Then check what the internal tools allow a support-authenticated session to do, and go cut that access off.

defendQuestions.question: Why is phone-verifiable, SMS-based second factor not enough against this kind of attack?
The first tempting story was a malicious insider. Why is that both wrong and harmful as a default explanation?
After containment, what one control change buys the most against phone-based credential attacks?

scenarios.lesson: People are part of your authentication chain. When a support process can be talked into a reset, attackers do not need your code to be broken — the fix is verification out-of-band, tighter least-privilege on internal tools, and a session-kill switch that works at incident speed. And assume attack, not malice, about your colleagues.
scenarios.realAction: In the real incident, attackers targeted a small number of employees by phone, manipulating them into providing credentials and/or resetting authentication; the attackers then used internal tools to post from, and delegate over, high-profile accounts, and the company cut off that access while limiting some account features platform-wide during response. We simplified: one containment arc, synthetic logs, no attack instructions — this scenario is defensive and educational only, like all our content.

scenarios.title: A quiet redeploy wakes up eight-year-old code
scenarios.story: You are the on-call engineer for a market-making desk's autonomous trading engine. At 9:30 am the market opened normally. At 9:33 the deployment pipeline finished last night's prep for tomorrow's new order-type feature — a routine change handled by an automated system. At 9:34 your order flow explodes and the desk's P&L starts moving like nothing anyone has seen. You are watching the dashboard while the desk stares at you.

services.name: Order gateway
services.role: your single pipe to the exchange

services.name: Trading engine
services.role: 8 replicas that decide what and when to send

services.name: Market feed
services.role: live prices from the exchange

services.name: Risk monitors
services.role: position limits and P&L display

timeline.text: SEV-1 from the desk: order rate is 100x normal on a handful of symbols and positions are building fast. The engine did exactly what its rules said — the rules changed under it.

events.text: The desk asks on the bridge: 'are we testing a new strategy?' Nobody is.
The exchange's market operations call about repeated quotes on 4 symbols from your firm.
P&L swings past the desk's worst-case chart. Every minute of noise costs money.

actions.label: Open the live order and risk dashboard

reveal.title: Order flow + risk, real time
lines: order rate: 100x normal, concentrated in 4 symbols
child orders: repeating in identical bursts, same size, same pattern
fills: genuinely filling — this is real money
overall market: choppy morning, but only our symbols show this pattern (noise, not signal)

reveal.title: smarts-engine/orders.log — 09:34 onward
lines: same parent order re-sent every few hundred milliseconds; hundreds of children each
log field 'position-complete': never set — the loop's exit condition never fires
the code path printing these lines identifies an old internal routine nobody recognizes on the bridge
engine replicas: all 8 report the same looping behavior

reveal.title: Deploy record — last night's prep
lines: prep purpose: enable tomorrow's new order type — no algorithm change intended
mechanism: reuse an EXISTING feature-flag id rather than define a new one
the flag id: defined in 2018 for a test routine, retired but never removed from the codebase
deploy status: rolled to 7 of 8 replicas (host 8 not in the batch)
deploy trigger: automated pipeline — no human on the desk touched anything this morning

reveal.title: Flag audit trail
lines: 2018 — flag created for an internal test routine whose exit condition needed manual completion marking
2021 — routine removed from the product backlog but its code stayed in the codebase
this morning — repurposing the id turned the dormant routine back ON in production
the test routine's exit path ('position-complete') was never wired to the live order gateway: matching the historical failure exactly

reveal.title: Replica-by-replica
lines: replicas 1-7: running this morning's prep, looping old routine, sending burst orders
replica 8: did NOT receive the deploy — it is idle-confused, still expecting flag state from yesterday
the deployed 7 agree with each other and disagree with reality
any fix that touches code must land on all 8 or the mismatch becomes its own incident

reveal.title: Feed health
lines: 2 symbols show 300ms slower quotes — tempting, but symmetric across all firms, not just us
our burst pattern exists only where our engine is sending
feed looks regular enough; this is a decoy in the noise on a choppy morning

actions.label: Stop sending: suspend the order gateway

reveal.title: Gateway suspended
lines: outbound orders stop; fills stop; the money-bleeding stops
exchange still visible; market data still healthy — you restart whenever ready
the desk exhales. Containment first, then cause

actions.label: Roll back last night's flag-prep change

reveal.title: Rollback of the prep change
lines: rollout plan re-runs against the same batch list: replicas 1-7 only
the dormant routine turns off on 7 replicas; replica 8 still disagrees with the fleet
if you halted here the week's real postmortem line would read 'partially applied changes are their own failure mode'

actions.label: Escalate: bring in market operations and the desk lead now

reveal.title: Fleet-wide escalation
lines: desk lead + exchange market-ops on the bridge; they can suspend your firm's symbols if this worsens
risk and comms teams start the regulatory clock and the client-call list
at this scale with an exchange watching you, nobody investigates alone

rootCauses.label: Last night's prep reused an old feature-flag id, switching ON dormant test code whose exit path was never functional in production — and it reached only 7 of 8 replicas
A breach or compromise moved market data or our own systems
A genuine market move drove the flow
A trader fat-fingered a parameter on the desk

fixes.label: Keep the gateway paused, roll the correct code to every replica including host 8, delete the dormant routine and its flag, and only then resume
fixes.note: Contains the bleeding first, then makes the whole fleet consistent, then removes the corpse so it can never wake again. Only now does order flow resume.

fixes.label: Roll back the change as it was deployed — on the same 7 replicas
fixes.note: The rollback plan inherits the same batch list. Replica 8 stays inconsistent and the fleet remains in mixed state — you paused the pain, not the cause.

fixes.label: Leave the flags alone and raise the risk limits so the flow fits within policy
fixes.note: You would be tuning the guardrails around a fire because the fire is inconvenient. The money keeps leaving, only slower and with permission.

hintLadder: The desk is shouting about flow, not latency. Ask which component decides what to send, and what could have changed its decision this morning without any new algorithm.
Nothing in the morning's noise answers this. The order logs and the deployment record are the quietest and highest-signal artifacts you own.

defendQuestions.question: Why did a 'feature-prep' change with no algorithm change send the engine haywire? Explain the flag reuse.
The rollback also went to 7 of 8 hosts. Why is a partial rollback its own failure?
What two guards from this incident generalize to any deploy system?

scenarios.lesson: Dead code with a live switch is not dead. Deploy tooling that reuses flags, code, names, or servers introduces coupling that outlives everything you knew when you wrote it — and any change that can land on some machines but not all is a split-brain waiting for a schedule. Kill the first symptom (stop sending), make the fleet consistent, and delete the bodies.
scenarios.realAction: In the real incident, a technician's deployment of new code to one production server was missed, an old flag was repurposed, and dormant eight-year-old code started sending millions of order statuses into the market; in under an hour the firm lost more money than it had earned in some entire years, and the public record (a regulator's order) treats it as a risk-control and deployment failure, not anyone's malice. We simplified the mechanics and made every number synthetic.
scenarios.inspiredByNote: Inspired by the publicly documented 2012 Knight Capital trading failure (SEC administrative record), simplified. Every number, log, and chart is synthetic.
